ELI15: You've probably seen diagrams of how DNA strands twist around each other and maybe you've heard how long the DNA inside each cell is. If you've wondered how it fits inside the cells, it's because most of the DNA is coiled up most of the time and gets only unfurled when it needs to be read. The double helix coils up like the old telephone cables and this coil is wound around puck shaped cylinders, which then coil up again into a twisted rope, see: http://www.nature.com/nrd/journal/v11/n5/images/nrd3674-f1.jpg

In that diagram the twisted rope is used to create chromosomes. What's the overlying structure after that? ¯\(ツ)/¯ We didn't know exactly until now. People thought that it was bunched up in a seemingly chaotic ball, because that's what it looked like.

Now in this work (http://www.nature.com/nature/journal/vaop/ncurrent/full/nature21429.html)) they've figured out how the chromosomes are puzzle pieces which fit together into the ball shape.

Why is this important? Now that we have a way of imaging that greater structure, we can study it further and maybe we'll find interactions with diseases, medicines etc.
